name: Simulating SU(2) Hadron dynamics on a 60 site lattice using 120 qubits
method:
Loop-string-hadron encoding into qubits, 1st order Trotterization, measurement error mitigation, measurement in Z-basis. differential measurement protocol. ### Method proof: SU(2) LSH hadron dynamics on 120 qubits We report a real-time quantum simulation of a non-Abelian lattice gauge theory: a $(1+1)$-dimensional SU(2) gauge theory with staggered fermions, encoded directly in the gauge-invariant loop-string-hadron (LSH) basis and implemented on IBM Boston. The submitted instance uses $N=60$ lattice sites, two qubits per site, and therefore 120 qubits. The main parameter set is $$ x=100,\qquad m/g=1,\qquad dt=0.0015, $$ with first-order Trotter evolution up to 20 steps. The physical task is to follow the real-time propagation of a localized hadronic excitation on top of the strong-coupling vacuum. Two product-state circuits are evolved: 1. a strong-coupling vacuum (SCV) circuit; 2. a centered-hadron circuit. The reported signal is obtained from the differential observable $$ \Delta n_f(r,t)=n_f^{\rm hadron}(r,t)-n_f^{\rm SCV}(r,t), $$ which removes the vacuum background and partially cancels hardware bias. The scalar observable used for the submitted data is $$ n_f(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{60}\Delta n_f(r,t). $$ ## Main result The main result for \(x=100\) is confined propagation of the SU(2) hadron signal with internal oscillation. The figure compares QPU data with tensor-network (TN), Pauli-propagation GPU (PP-GPU), and Pauli-propagation CPU (PP-CPU) calculations. It also shows particle-number dynamics, symmetry diagnostics, meson-gap extraction, and runtime comparison.
Main result for x=100: confined SU(2) hadron propagation with internal oscillation, comparison among QPU, TN, PP-GPU, and PP-CPU, symmetry diagnostics, meson gap, and quantum/classical runtime comparison.

## Qubit Hamiltonian At each lattice site \(r\), the two binary LSH string-end occupations $n_i(r), n_o(r)\in$ \{0,1\} are encoded as $$ n_i(r)=\frac{1-Z_i(r)}{2},\qquad n_o(r)=\frac{1-Z_o(r)}{2}. $$ The dimensionless Hamiltonian is $$ W=H_E+\mu H_M+xH_I,\qquad \mu=2(m/g)\sqrt{x}. $$ For \(x=100\) and \(m/g=1\), \(\mu=20\). The circuit implements the large-\(x\) LSH approximation. Up to irrelevant constants, the approximate electric term is $$ H_E^{\rm approx}=\frac{A}{4}\sum_r\left[I-Z_o(r)+Z_i(r)-Z_i(r)Z_o(r)\right], \qquad A=\frac{\ell_i}{2}+\frac{3}{4},$$ where \(\ell_i\) is the chosen large incoming flux parameter. The approximate mass term is $$H_M^{\rm approx}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_r(-1)^r\left[Z_i(r)+Z_o(r)\right].$$ The interaction term maps to nearest-neighbor $XX+YY$ hopping on the $i$- and $o$-chains: $$ H_I^{\rm approx}=-\sum_{r=0}^{N-2}\left[X_i(r)X_i(r+1)+Y_i(r)Y_i(r+1)\right]-\sum_{r=0}^{N-2}\left[X_o(r)X_o(r+1)+Y_o(r)Y_o(r+1)\right].$$ The first-order Trotter step is $$ e^{-i\mu dt H_M}\,e^{-idtH_E}\,e^{-ixdtH_I}, $$ with $$ xdt=0.15,\qquad \mu dt=0.03. $$ The diagonal $Z$ and $ZZ$ terms are implemented by phase rotations. The hopping terms are implemented through $XX+YY$-type two-qubit gates together with SWAP layers required by the hardware layout. ## Initial states and observables Both initial states are computational-basis product states prepared using only $X$ gates. The SCV has alternating site occupations $$ (00,11,00,11,\ldots,00,11), $$ and the centered-hadron state is obtained by replacing the central SCV block by a localized hadronic excitation. The exact 120-bit initialization strings are fixed by the submitted QASM circuit files. The local staggered fermion number is reconstructed from Pauli-\(Z\) measurements: $$ n_f(r)= \begin{cases} 1-\frac{1}{2}\left[Z_i(r)+Z_o(r)\right], & r\ \text{even},\\\\[4pt] 1+\frac{1}{2}\left[Z_i(r)+Z_o(r)\right], & r\ \text{odd}. \end{cases} $$ The conserved global charge is $$ Q=\sum_r\left[n_i(r)+n_o(r)\right] =60-\frac{1}{2}\sum_r\left[Z_i(r)+Z_o(r)\right], $$ with exact value \(Q=60\) in the submitted sector. We use this as a symmetry-violation diagnostic. For the submitted \(t=20\) instance, IBM Boston gives $$ n_f(20)_{\rm QPU}=-0.07723426024, $$ and $$ Q_{\rm QPU}(20)=59.99402699, $$ so that $$ |Q_{\rm QPU}(20)-60|=0.00597301. $$ The IBM Boston runs used 10,000 shots per circuit and measurement-error mitigation only. ## Circuit files and circuit structure The submitted QASM circuit files are available here: [https://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/tree/main/data/observable-estimations/circuit-models/su2_lsh_hadron_dynamics](https://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/tree/main/data/observable-estimations/circuit-models/su2_lsh_hadron_dynamics) Because the observable is differential, reproducing the reported signal requires both circuit families: the SCV evolution circuits and the centered-hadron evolution circuits. The submitted files include the relevant $N=60$, 120-qubit, $x=100$, $dt=0.0015$ instances at selected Trotter depths, including the primary 20-step instance.
Representative circuit figures. Top: elementary gate blocks used in the construction. Middle: example compiled circuit layout. Bottom: corresponding QASM-style circuit pattern.

## Classical comparisons We compare the QPU data with three classical calculations. **Tensor network (TN).** The TN benchmark uses an in-house MPS/MPO simulation of the fuller LSH Hamiltonian with two-site TDVP, bosonic cutoff $j_{\max}=5/2$, and maximum bond dimension 200. This TN calculation evolves a less-approximated LSH Hamiltonian using TDVP. It is therefore not identical to the Trotterized large-$x$ circuit implemented on the QPU; consequently, even a noiseless ideal QPU circuit is not expected to coincide exactly with the TN trajectory. **Pauli propagation on CPU (PP-CPU).** PP-CPU performs noiseless Heisenberg-picture propagation of the circuit-level observable. For $x=100$, the safe non-truncated Pauli-term bound is 12,500 terms. **Pauli propagation on GPU (PP-GPU).** PP-GPU uses NVIDIA cuQuantum/cuPauliProp with coefficient cutoff $$ \epsilon=10^{-5}, $$ which gives a controlled circuit-level approximation while reducing memory and runtime. ## Runtime comparison For the explicit $x=100$ instances, the wall-clock comparison is: | Trotter step | QPU time (s) | TN time (s) | PP-CPU time (s) | PP-GPU time (s) | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 5 | 20 | 584.092 | 477.4471 | 547.5810 | | 10 | 20 | 4936.112 | 1111.2079 | 1186.1290 | | 15 | 20 | 11300.992 | 1798.2811 | 1990.1430 | | 20 | 20 | 8949.110 | 2484.3693 | 2930.4400 | The QPU wall-clock time is approximately constant per submitted circuit, while the classical methods grow substantially with Trotter depth. ## Additional circuit-MPS check A circuit-level MPS simulation using Quimb was also tested for the 120-qubit Trotterized circuit. With cutoff $10^{-9}$ and maximum bond dimension $\sim 200$, the simulation remained controlled at early Trotter steps but developed increasing truncation effects at later times. The MPS wave-function norm decreased significantly by step 20. This suggests that improved tensor-network strategies exploiting the effective ladder geometry are an important direction for future classical comparison. ## Links Preprint: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.18080](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.18080) QASM circuit files: [https://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/tree/main/data/observable-estimations/circuit-models/su2_lsh_hadron_dynamics](https://github.com/quantum-advantage-tracker/quantum-advantage-tracker.github.io/tree/main/data/observable-estimations/circuit-models/su2_lsh_hadron_dynamics) Supporting circuit repository: [https://github.com/indrakshir/LSH-IBM](https://github.com/indrakshir/LSH-IBM) Raw experimental data: [https://github.com/mathew0036/lsh_data](https://github.com/mathew0036/lsh_data)
